name: Kavalan
catalog_quote: Kavalan words are stressed on the final syllable. This can be seen in a number of the pitch tracks presented so far in this Chapter, where the F0 peak of a pitch accent is aligned with the vowel of the final syllable. ... sources.citation: Hsieh, Fuhui 謝富惠. 2018. 噶瑪蘭語語法概論 [Outline of Kavalan grammar], 2nd ed. (臺灣南島語言叢書 11). New Taipei City: Council of Indigenous Peoples. 4+xviii+210 pp. Open flipbook: https://alilin.cip.gov.tw/Book/564 (page images.../ebook/17419802765b6abd1e859b7/books/images/2/)
sources.quote: 在噶瑪蘭語中，重音固定落在詞的倒數第一音節。即使是加上動貌記號或是代名詞依附詞後，整個詞組的重音仍落在最後一個音節 ('In Kavalan, stress falls fixed on the last syllable of the word. Even when aspect markers or pronominal clitics are added, the stress of the whole group still falls on the last syllable'), ex. (2-1) pukún → pukun=pa=ikú.

sources.citation: Moriguchi, Tsunekazu. 1983. An inquiry into Kbalan phonology. Journal of Asian and African Studies 26: 202-219. https://tufs.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/1758/files/
sources.quote: 'the accent in Kbalan is the length, which is indicated by the shortness of the penultimate syllable. Two of the other prominences, that is, pitch and stress are not distinctive phonemically. The stress/amplitude automatically falls on the ultimate syllable'; 'the stress, which is not distinctive and automatically assigned to the ultimate syllable, falls on the latter part of the vowels in the succession, when there are two successive vowels in final syllable.'
sources.locator: p.216 sec VII Accent; also p.215-216 on VV-final syllables

sources.citation: Moriguchi, Tsunekazu. 1982. Some notes on accent in Kbalan: A minority aboriginal language in Formosa. Journal of Asian and African Studies (ILCAA, Tokyo) 24: 120-132. https://tufs.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/1749/files/
sources.quote: 'The stress in Kbalan words is usually predictable and fixed at the end of the final syllable. As shown in Fig. 1 the primary stress falls on the ultimate syllable.' (amplitude + pitch traces of [saBo?] 'cool' vs [sa:Bo?] 'pestle'); the distinctive 'accent' he argues for is penultimate vowel length, not stress position. p.124: Li (1981) 'reports that neither stress nor length is phonemic. The stress is fixed on the ultimate syllable and the penultimate syllable is lengthened.'
sources.locator: pp.126-127 sec IV(iii)(1); p.124 (report of Li 1981)
